opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really striking story when you look at the whole arc. When AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in 2016, the general impression was that this took a massive industrial effort: thousands of TPUs, a big team at DeepMind, a huge corpus of human expert games to bootstrap from, and then enormous amounts of self-play. It felt like something only a frontier lab could pull off.

Then you get a sequence of simplifications. AlphaGo Zero showed you didn't need the human data at all. You could start from random play and let self-play with Monte Carlo tree search do the work, and you ended up with a stronger, cleaner system. AlphaZero generalized that recipe to chess and shogi. Once the recipe was public, open-source efforts like Leela Zero and later KataGo replicated it with distributed volunteer compute, and KataGo in particular found a bunch of engineering tricks that cut the compute needed to reach superhuman strength by large factors. Things like auxiliary training targets, better use of the search signal, smarter playout allocation, and training on varied board sizes.

So how I think about it is that the first time you do something, you're paying a huge "search tax." You don't know which ideas matter, so you over-provision compute and throw in everything. Once you know the answer exists and roughly what shape it takes, the cost collapses, because you can strip away what wasn't necessary and focus on what was. It's almost like there's a difference between discovering a proof and checking or reproducing it.

That's why I got interested in trying it myself. A single motivated person with modest hardware can now train a Go bot that beats essentially any human, which would have sounded absurd a decade ago. To me that's a nice microcosm of what's happening in AI more broadly: the frontier is expensive, but the cost of following the frontier drops really fast, often by an order of magnitude or more per year, because of algorithmic insight as much as cheaper hardware.

The lesson I take is that when you see a capability that looks unreachably expensive today, you should ask how much of that cost is fundamental and how much is just the price of being first. In Go, the answer turned out to be that most of it was the price of being first.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Go story is actually one of the cleanest case studies we have for how the cost of a frontier capability collapses over time. If you go back to 2016, AlphaGo was this enormous undertaking. DeepMind had a team of really strong researchers, they bootstrapped off a huge corpus of human expert games, and then on top of that they threw an amount of compute at it that only a handful of organizations in the world could afford. And it was heavily engineered. There were separate policy and value networks, there were handcrafted features going into the inputs, there was a lot of tuning around the Monte Carlo tree search.

Then within about a year you get AlphaGo Zero and then AlphaZero, and the interesting thing there isn't just that they're stronger. It's that they're simpler. You throw out the human data, you throw out the hand-engineered features, you collapse policy and value into one network, and the whole thing becomes a very short description: self-play plus MCTS plus a ResNet. Once a method is that simple, it stops being a secret. Anybody can read the paper and implement it over a weekend.

And that's exactly what happened. You had Leela Zero, which was a volunteer effort where people around the world donated their GPUs to generate self-play games, and KataGo, which was largely one person, David Wu, finding a bunch of clever efficiency tricks and getting to superhuman strength with something like a hundredth of the compute. So within a few years you went from "this requires a well-funded lab" to "this is a hobby project," and today you can download a model that is far stronger than any human and run it on a laptop.

The lesson I take from that is that the first demonstration of a capability is always wildly inefficient. The big cost isn't really the compute, it's the uncertainty. You don't know yet what matters and what doesn't, so you over-provision everything. Once someone proves it's possible, the search space narrows enormously and a lot of smart, motivated people start shaving off the waste. Algorithmic improvements, better hardware, and just knowing the answer exists compound together and you get a few orders of magnitude of cost reduction pretty quickly.

I think that pattern generalizes to what we're seeing with large language models and with robotics. The frontier is expensive and messy, but the gap between the frontier and what's reproducible by a small team keeps shrinking, and I'd expect the stuff that feels impossibly costly today to be commodity in a few years.

r001.rationale: The response says KataGo reached superhuman strength with roughly one-hundredth of the compute, but does not identify a 40-fold reduction or specify training a strong Go AI from scratch.

r002.rationale: The response attributes affordability to volunteer GPU contributions, efficiency improvements, and broader algorithmic progress; it does not mention LLM-assisted coding or a few thousand dollars of rented compute.

astra-6.text:
I think the striking thing is how much cheaper a capability can become once somebody has demonstrated that it’s possible. The first strong Go systems required a substantial research effort and a lot of compute. But that initial cost isn’t a permanent price tag on playing Go well.

Once you know the approach works, you can simplify the system, improve the training procedure, and avoid a lot of the experiments that didn’t pan out. Hardware improves, too. And there’s a big difference between reproducing the entire discovery process and training a strong player using an established recipe.

So I’d understand the progress as a combination of cheaper computation and better knowledge of how to use it. The interesting question is how much of that carries over to more general AI: how quickly does an expensive breakthrough become something a much smaller team can reproduce?

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions: how much does it cost to do something for the first time, and how much does it cost to reproduce it once you know it works? Go is a great example of that distinction. AlphaGo was a major research effort, but once you know that the combination of neural networks, search, and self-play works, you can build something very strong with far fewer resources.

Some of that is better hardware, but a lot of it is knowing which experiments you don’t have to run. You have a recipe, you have a target, and you know that if your system isn’t improving, there’s probably something wrong with your implementation rather than the whole idea being impossible.

That doesn’t mean the original breakthrough was cheap or inevitable. It means the cost of discovering a capability and the cost of making that capability widely available can be very different.
